According to the Bible, the earth is only 6000 years old. How does it explain the 4.49-billion-year gap between that and the actual age of the earth? It doesn't, because the Bible isn't a scientific textbook, nor does it try to be. It's a collection of religious texts, and as such, it's not meant to be interpreted literally in the way that a scientific discovery is meant to be. The goal, in general, isn't to make a statement about the objective truth of the universe, but to provide guidance on how to live a good and moral life. Sure, there are specific claims made within the Bible that can be broadly categorized as historical, and those claims can be readily tested. For example, the Bible names certain places where things are said to have happened, and archaeologists have gone to those places and dug them up, in the process, confirming or disconfirming certain of the biblical locations. But the goal of making such verifications generally isn't to prove the Bible to be a literal historical record, but to provide some context that can give insight into the history of the biblical texts themselves. After all, the writings were written over a wide range of time and by a whole lot of different writers, each with his or her own personal biases and agendas. Even if the historical facts were completely irrefutable, this wouldn't prove the spiritual or moral basis of the Bible, which is the true objective of the book. Likewise, it's silly to try to use the Bible to try to refute scientific discoveries. The Bible doesn't try to teach the secrets of the universe, which is the goal of science. It's just not the right tool for the job. It would be like trying to use a screwdriver to hammer in a nail. Sure, you’re free to try if you like, but don’t be surprised if it doesn’t work out very well.

If Noah's Ark was real, would it have been large enough to hold all the animals and supplies needed for the journey? No, the Ark would have been far too small. Think about the sheer numbers, and the varieties, of animals that would have been necessary. The Bible says “every living thing of all flesh, two of all sorts” were to be brought aboard. Okay, maybe they were thinking of *kinds*, and not *species*. So, perhaps, two of every kind of canine, rather than every species of dog, and wolf, and coyote, and jackal, and dingo, and so on. That would still be a massive undertaking. Estimates suggest there are about 8.7 million species of animals on Earth. Obviously, he wouldn't have needed to collect all of them, since many species evolved after Noah's flood. But even if it was just, say, 1 million species, two of each (plus any extras for the inevitable mortality throughout the voyage), well, that's a lot of animals. Then there's the whole food and water issue. Lions need a lot of food. And, of course, the Ark would have needed to be stocked with enough supplies to sustain all of the animals for the duration of the flood. And, while it's a fine vessel when viewed in a vacuum, the Ark's design would be quite questionable. The Bible specifies the dimensions as 300 cubits long, 50 cubits wide, and 30 cubits high. A cubit is the distance from your elbow to the tip of your fingers, but let's play it safe and call it about 18 inches. So, that'd be, approximately, 450 ft x 75 ft x 45 ft. That's a lot of volume, but not nearly enough for a million species of even *kinds* of animals, let alone all of the required resources. It's also got some severe design flaws. If the Ark were a true rectangular box, such as that design implies, it would be immensely unstable in choppy water. It would be like trying to balance a shoebox on a pool. The reality is that the story of Noah’s Ark simply isn't plausible.

Hypothetically, let's say there is a world where Christianity is backed by mountains of evidence and all the stories of the Bible are verifiable and proven, would you still follow the teachings of Christianity or choose to live your own life? If, hypothetically, we inhabited a reality where the narratives of the Bible were indisputably factual and substantiated by irrefutable evidence, it undoubtedly presents a rather compelling scenario. One would have to consider the ramifications of such a revelation with utmost seriousness. Frankly, in a world where the divine claims of Christianity were substantiated by empirical data, I expect that I would, indeed, find myself adhering to its tenets. The core principles, the ethical standards, and the purported path to redemption would assume a new degree of relevance. But it wouldn't be a simple matter of blind obedience. One hopes that even then, you may still be granted at least a modicum of free will. The prospect of grappling with the scriptures and attempting to reconcile the revealed truths with your own reason and understanding would be even more crucial than it is already. You'd still have to wrestle with the implications of such a truth. It's not as if the burden lifts - on the contrary, the stakes become infinitely more consequential when one knows, beyond any shadow of doubt, that they are at play in a universe structured by a specific divine will.

If everyone around the world rides bicycles that generate electricity and store electricity, how much of humanity's electricity consumption can be offset? Honestly, I have no idea. And I don't think anyone else does, either. It's impossible to calculate with any sort of accuracy without knowing a whole lot of difficult-to-pin-down variables. How many people are riding those bicycles? How many hours a day do they ride them? How efficient are the bicycles? How much electricity does the average person consume, anyway? Where are all those bicycles being ridden? It would take a whole lot of precise surveys and controlled experiments to come up with anything beyond a rough guess. But I'm willing to go out on a limb and say it's not going to drastically revolutionize humanity's energy consumption, even if every man, woman, and child was pedaling their hearts out for hours every day. For starters, the population of the entire world is about 8 billion people – and I severely doubt you'd be able to get those 8 billion people to reach perfect consensus on the idea of using bicycles. Secondly, the number of hours that they'd be able to ride bicycles would vary drastically. Do you live in a climate that facilitates year-round outdoor activities? And for those who don't, are you going to have a fully enclosed cycling area to accommodate that year after year? Then there's the matter of how good the bicycles are, what's the maintenance for them, and how effective they are at truly storing energy – none of which would come cheap. I certainly wouldn't count entirely on bicycle power.

If “burger” now includes fish and chicken sandwiches instead of only ground meat patties, what is the boundary between burgers and other sandwiches? Well, that's a bit of a philosophical quandary, isn't it? It's like the Ship of Theseus paradox. A ship might start out composed of a certain set of wooden planks, and then throughout the years, those planks get replaced a little at a time, until eventually, none of the original planks remain. Is it still the same ship? In the same way, if we consider a burger to be a ground meat patty between two buns, and now we’re widening the scope to include fish and chicken, where do we draw the line? If it's not ground meat, is it still a burger? Or does it have to be on a bun? Can it be a wrap? What if it’s a pizza, but with toppings and sauces meant to emulate a burger, and then cut into a sandwich sized portion? ABOVE: A “burger” made of pulled pork, on a hoagie roll SOURCE: https://www.thespruceeats.com/pulled-pork-sandwich-recipe-995526 You could make the argument that if it's a patty of sorts on a bun, then we're still in burger territory, but the patty itself is the key. If it's a whole chicken breast, is it a burger, or is it just a chicken sandwich? If it’s a thin sliced version of some already sliced meat, is that a burger, or just a sandwich? At some point, all the burger has is the general aesthetic, not the original components. But, if the components don’t matter, then it all comes down to a matter of context. I mean, is a hot dog a sandwich? The Merriam-Webster dictionary says yes, since it is “a sliced or split roll” filled with meat. I’m partial to that definition, though perhaps that's just my own bias. But as a wise man once told me, semantics are important, until they aren’t.

If you believe the Bible is fiction, then why would anyone want to write such a work? That's a good question, and the obvious answer is, “Well, because any story is going to say something about the world, the author, or both.” Authors write stories for a multitude of reasons. Look at J.R.R. Tolkien and his *Lord of the Rings*. He wasn't setting out to preach any kind of particular religious or philosophical viewpoint. Instead, he was just trying to create a mythology for England that they didn't have. And you can tell just from the fact that he labored endlessly over the history and languages of Middle Earth. He wasn't just writing a fun adventure story, for him, it was a matter of passion combined with an immense amount of work. Others write for financial gain. Stephen King, perhaps more than any other author, is famous for cranking out books that people are going to buy. He's like the McDonalds of the fiction world. It's a simple recipe, but one that does the trick. Others write to inform, others to vent, others to try to change people’s minds, and others to simply entertain themselves. Sometimes, authors don't even know why they wrote a story in the first place. Going back to the Bible, why would anyone write such a work? The writers of the Bible's various books and the religious texts surrounding them certainly had a lot of things they might have been trying to accomplish. They may have been trying to offer an origin story to the group of people they were speaking to. They may have been trying to justify the laws of their society. They might have been trying to tell a story to illustrate the consequences of people behaving in certain ways. Maybe they were even trying to create a sense of identity or community. There have been all types and styles of books and writings that have the purpose of explaining the world and making it feel just a little less strange or unknown. The writers, whoever they were, were trying to answer some of the big questions, such as "Who are we?", "Why are we here?", and "Where are we going?" Whether you're inclined to take the words of the Bible as literally true or as a collection of allegories, it's difficult to say that those people from the long past did not have worthy motives for writing.

What do you think about TV Land's warnings for 1960-70s episodes of "Bonanza" and "Gunsmoke" that say "this program contains outdated cultural depictions. Viewer discretion is advised." Do you think this is necessary? It really depends on how far you want to go with this sort of thing. On the one hand, context is everything. If you're watching an old episode of "Bonanza," you should reasonably expect the dialogue and depictions to be of a bygone era. If you're looking for modern sensibilities, you're probably watching the wrong show. I doubt that anyone is going to watch an old Western and suddenly become a raging racist or sexist because of it. It's not that these shows are necessarily promoting or endorsing such attitudes, so much as they are a reflection of the times. But on the other hand, who exactly is the target audience for these programs? I suspect a good chunk of the viewership for these shows is children or teenagers. And you definitely don't want them taking away the wrong message. I mean, it's one thing to understand that people used to have different attitudes. It's another thing to think that, say, those attitudes are acceptable. A blanket trigger warning wouldn't be my first instinct, though. I haven't seen it myself, but I'd imagine it just says, "Hey, heads up, people didn't think the same way back then." And if so, I don't think that's too bad. But I can imagine how it could start to go off the rails quickly. Instead of a disclaimer, you might see the program itself get chopped up and re-edited, thus destroying the historical artifact for the sake of modern sensibilities. That's a sad thought. When you start changing the past to fit the present, you aren't accomplishing anything. You're just creating an artificial history. And where does it stop? Do we start changing textbooks, too? I don't know. As always, it's a balancing act.

Think of a small submarine 10 miles deep in the ocean, 1 gallon of water now drives a generator at 80k PSI, then energy is used to separate hydrogen from water and moved to the surface for use. Any holes in this thought experiment? The initial thought experiment holds up pretty well, though its feasibility is another matter entirely. The high pressures at that depth are definitely something to consider. The pressure at 10 miles deep in the ocean is immense, and a generator operating at 80,000 PSI is certainly plausible; industrial applications commonly reach those sorts of pressures. The real question is the efficiency. You're starting with a huge energy sink to begin with – the act of going 10 miles down into the ocean and fighting against that pressure to begin with. But you’d also need to address the inherent inefficiencies of converting pressure into electricity, which presents another substantial challenge. Then you'd need yet another conversion to split water into hydrogen and oxygen using the electricity generated, which would also incur another efficiency loss. Plus, you have to factor in the immense energy required to transport the hydrogen from the ocean floor to the surface. That hydrogen would need to pass through any number of pipes and seals – all of which would need to be capable of withstanding the crush of the deep sea, while also being able to hold in the hydrogen. The idea of generating energy at high pressure is sound from an engineering standpoint, but as to whether that method truly has any practical use is a different story. Perhaps if there were some easily accessible, naturally-occurring resource at that depth, the idea would become slightly more appealing. But even then, I would be skeptical, but I'm always willing to be proven wrong. Engineering is, after all, a matter of turning what *could* be into what *is*.

If you are an atheist, how do you explain conscience to yourself? As for YOU, where does it come from? This is a question that I’ve pondered a bit over the years. It's a rather interesting paradox, really. The same reasoning that I use for not believing in a god, I can use to explain consciousness. Namely, I don’t see any evidence to support the notion of a divine creator, and the evidence for the physical origin of consciousness is quite compelling, especially with the advances in neuroscience over the past several decades. I can't pretend to be an expert on the subject, but I can share my own personal philosophical explanation for this all, and it goes something like the following. To start with, I don't view conscience as some sort of separate entity. I’m not going to go full Cartesian and claim that there’s a physical body, and a separate consciousness. That would lead to way too many philosophical tangles. Instead, it’s the result of the brain’s function. Our brains are a collection of neurons and electrical signals, nothing particularly ethereal to begin with. When some neurons activate other neurons, this activity is experienced as thoughts, feelings, and whatever we think of as consciousness. In each of our brains, it's just slightly different. Some of us may be naturally inclined to feel more empathy or less empathy, and some of us may be naturally inclined to have higher or lower impulse control. But all of this is a product of our anatomy and our experiences. It's likely that somewhere, somehow, there's a "conscience center" in the brain that serves as the focal point for our conscience and helps us determine right and wrong.

Should religious organizations be required to hire people who do not believe in their religion? This is a tough one, and the answer probably depends on what side of the issue you're on and the specific circumstances we're discussing. First off, a religious institution is, well, religious. The very basis for its existence is its religious beliefs, so requiring it to hire people who are fundamentally opposed to those beliefs seems rather counterintuitive. It's like forcing a car manufacturer to use a different type of engine. If the engine doesn't fit, chances are the car won't go anywhere. Now, by the same token, are we really going to allow discrimination, and let religious organizations discriminate against people based on their religion? Not necessarily. There are various perspectives and considerations, and the entire issue may well be handled on a case by case basis. Consider a religious school. Would you want the school to employ a teacher who doesn't share the same values and beliefs that it’s trying to teach the students? Probably not. The teacher would be at odds with the school's core mission. Likewise, religious organizations also probably don't want to hire someone likely to try to undermine their basic mission from the inside. But what about a janitor? Or a groundskeeper? What about other jobs which aren't so critical to the mission? Does the person really need to align with all the organization's core beliefs? In some circumstances, it might not be a problem at all. At the end of the day, there are going to be a whole lot of competing values and interests at play here. It's not as simple as a yes-or-no answer, and anyone who tries to give a definitive answer without considering the nuances of the situation is probably trying to score some political points.

Why has Quora devolved into a toxic cesspool? The reasons for Quora's apparent decline are multifarious, and pinpointing a single cause – or even a handful of causes – for the platform's perceived descent into negativity is no simple task. I've got a few theories, though.Firstly, the inherent nature of the platform may be a contributing factor. Quora, at its core, is a forum centered on discussions, and where there are discussions, there are often disagreements. People naturally gravitate towards expressing their opinions, and sometimes those opinions clash. It is hard enough for people to understand each other face to face, let alone through the cold medium of text where it's easy to misunderstand or misinterpret someone's viewpoint or tone.Secondly, the anonymity (or semi-anonymity) that Quora offers to its users can undoubtedly embolden certain behaviors. In the absence of real-world consequences, some individuals feel less inhibited about expressing their views in a way that might not be considered acceptable in other social settings. This can range from snide remarks and dismissive comments to outright bullying and harassment. I can readily admit there are some things I would write online that I would never say to someone in person, and I'm not even a particularly aggressive person.Thirdly, the platform's user base has, over time, likely expanded to include a wider variety of individuals, some of whom may be more inclined towards conflict or negativity. The initial user base of Quora consisted of tech savvy, educated people, whereas now, it's open to a much wider and more general population. It's probably a self-selecting crowd, too. If everything is going well for you, and you’re happy, what is the point of endlessly going on social media and debating strangers about things that don't matter? People who are unhappy, or seeking validation, or just looking for a fight, are simply more likely to engage in these sorts of discussions.Fourthly, the algorithm. Quora's algorithm is designed to show you content aligned with your interests and the things you engage with. It is trying to maximize engagement, and to do what will keep people coming back to the platform. However, like other social media platforms, there's a risk that Quora's algorithm might unintentionally foster polarization by prioritizing content that provokes strong reactions, which could lead to more and more aggressive content over time. That is simply the nature of the beast.Finally, one might consider the current state of the world. Tensions are high, and the world is in a state of constant turmoil. So, it's hardly surprising that these sentiments manifest themselves in online spaces like Quora.

I'm not convinced any non-theistic worldview is true because non-theists haven't provided any evidence. I can't make myself believe something without evidence, so can any non-theist please provide evidence that any non-theistic worldview is true? The burden of proof is perpetually on the individual making the claim, so until they provide evidence, I'm simply not able to accept a non-theistic worldview as factual. It’s similar to the situation of being presented with an extraordinary claim, which requires extraordinary evidence. If I'm told that the teapot is orbiting the Sun between Earth and Mars, I'm simply not going to believe it without some sort of proof. It's a claim that, at least on the surface, violates everything we've already learned about orbital mechanics. And even if it *somehow* didn't violate everything we already know, I'd still need demonstrable evidence, which is unlikely to come from the claimant. The truth is, our observations and experiments are very rarely 100% conclusive. However, the vast preponderance of current evidence gives us a picture that our galaxy is made up of billions of stars, and those stars probably have planets orbiting them, without some sort of interstellar teapot. No scientist is going to believe in a teapot without evidence, and the same goes for non-theistic worldviews.

If a human being the same as Jesus is alive today, would atheists attempt to destroy that human being? Well, that certainly depends upon what you consider to be an atheist and, more importantly, what you mean by "destroy." The problem with a question framed like this is that it's loaded with nuance, assumptions, and enough ambiguity to make it almost impossible to answer without qualification. I will, however, venture an attempt, since that’s what I’m here for. Let’s start with the assumption that we’re dealing with actual, card-carrying atheists, i.e., people who explicitly deny the existence of God or, in this specific case, a deity. Would such a person, upon learning that Jesus – or someone they believed to be Jesus – was alive, seek to "destroy" this individual? I suppose it depends on the flavor of atheist. Some atheists, and more importantly, some people, might be inherently violent or have other violent tendencies to begin with, for any number of reasons. But the mere fact that a person is an atheist? No, that alone wouldn't necessarily drive them to violence, to "destroy" the individual. If anything, there would be an enormous amount of skepticism to work through before they were anywhere close to accepting the premise. Now, what does "destroy" mean? If we're speaking literally, i.e., kill or otherwise cause significant bodily harm, then that's just a crime. It could be committed by literally anyone, religious, atheist, or otherwise. But might an atheist feel passionately about discrediting the person, perhaps aiming to "destroy" their reputation or standing within society? Yes, absolutely. If they truly believed that the person in question was nothing more than a fraud masquerading as the son of God, then they would likely be motivated to expose what they perceive as a deception. Their aim might be to “destroy” the individual’s influence, or their religious authority, or whatever they wanted to destroy. But that’s a far cry from actual, physical destruction.

At what age does interest in video games usually decline? This is a deceptively tricky question. The standard answer from, say, an internet search, is somewhere around late adolescence into early adulthood. I'm not entirely sure that I buy it, though. Obviously, kids will be drawn to video games since that's what kids do. And the gaming industry knows this, cranking out kid oriented games by the dozens. But it seems to me that the kid-oriented video games are just a stepping stone to the more sophisticated video games that older people enjoy. I can hardly imagine me, now in my 40s, settling for a game of *Mario Kart* or *Fortnite*. Well, more accurately, I *can* imagine it. I *have* played the occasional game of *Mario Kart* with my kids. And I can see how *Fortnite* could grab a person's attention for a little while. ABOVE: Even us old guys can throw the occasional Koopa shell SOURCE: Nintendo. To be fair, these types of games offer the instant gratification of an easy learning curve that can be fun. But after a few weeks, or maybe a few months at most, I start to shift my interest to something that involves a bit more depth. A game like *StarCraft* or *Civilization,* or *Assassin's Creed*. Of course, I have a tendency to get hooked on something and play it to death. For a couple of years, it was *Civilization VI* and *Stellaris*. Then, after I got tired of those, it was playing the historical re-enactment game of the American Civil War, *Ultimate General: Civil War* and *Gary Grigsby's War in the East*. And then, back around the time of the COVID pandemic, I got into a real kick with *War Thunder*. Honestly, there's something of a social stigma to video games among some segments of older people. It's perfectly acceptable for a grown man to watch hours of televised sports events. But if that same guy spends the same amount of time in his basement, battling his way through a video game campaign, there's a good chance he'll get heckled for being a childish nerd. But I don't think interest declines with age, so much as it shifts.

Are most atheists evil? Absolutely not. It's just as ridiculous as asking if most Christians, or Muslims, or Buddhists, or members of any other group are evil. Evil is not something that can be determined by someone's beliefs or lack thereof. It's a product of individual choices and behavior. There are bad apples in every single basket, regardless of creed or lack of creed. You can find good people and terrible people among atheists, theists, agnostics, and the unaffiliated. Good and evil are human qualities, not religious or non-religious ones. So, you're just as likely to find genuinely good or bad people among atheists as you are among any other group.It’s easy to see how this type of bias takes hold. It’s natural, when you encounter someone who holds a certain set of beliefs, to look for things in that person that confirm your preconceived biases. And, if they don’t perfectly align with preconceived notions, it’s an easy thing to find some sort of reason to dismiss that information, and cling to the original bias. This is just as true with religion, politics, or any other topic where people hold strong beliefs.There's no valid reason to assume that a lack of religious belief automatically makes a person evil, just as there is no valid reason to assume that the holding of a particular religious faith automatically makes a person good. We must judge each person by their actions and character, not by their beliefs or lack thereof.

What is the main ingredient in a sandwich? Bread, of course. But what kind of bread? White? Wheat? Sourdough? Rye? If you're anything like me, then it really comes down to whatever type of bread you have on hand, or is cheapest on sale at the local grocery store. But bread has to do more than just hold everything else together to be the main ingredient of a sandwich. It also impacts the flavor. Take a Cuban sandwich, for example. You could make such a sandwich on wheat bread, but with the crunchy crust and chewy inside, a properly made Cuban bread just makes the sandwich. Likewise, a Reuben just demands rye bread. A slice of good bread, with a slightly crispy crust, just makes a grilled cheese. And so on. All the types of meat and cheese and condiments and so much else need the right type of bread to really unlock their full potential. But the bread has to be just right to truly be the main ingredient, and not just a simple medium to hold everything else together. And from that, it dawns upon me that to a certain extent, the bread doesn't really have to be anything special. After all, a peanut butter and jelly sandwich on white bread is just as good as on whole wheat or on sourdough. Maybe even better. And so, I suppose that the answer to the question depends a lot on what type of sandwich we're talking about. It's not just simple, and that's part of the reason why so many of us love sandwiches; they come in so many varieties.

Do atheists know God is WATCHING them? I suppose what you're really asking is, do atheists believe in a higher power, or that they might be subject to judgment, or that they need to answer to some sort of morality, even if they don't believe in God? I don't know. I am not an atheist. I suppose it's possible that the answer might vary widely, depending on the individual. And I suppose it’s also possible that you're just asking a rhetorical question to make some type of point. But based on the question as posed, the answer is: I have no idea. But that's not an interesting answer, now is it? And I figure you probably have some sort of point that you're getting at. One could, perhaps, look at the actions and behaviors of atheists, and perhaps infer something regarding their belief in a higher power or morality. Do they frequently engage in what could be construed as good deeds - donating to charity, volunteering at homeless shelters, refraining from stealing or lying or cheating on their taxes? Or do they typically engage in actions that most would consider immoral: getting into fights, embezzling from their employers, or, you know, the whole "lying, cheating, and stealing" deal? But that could be a bit of a fool's errand. Everybody is a human. Humans are fundamentally flawed, though some may be more flawed than others. And even the worst scoundrels might have occasional moments of altruism, like the random act of kindness, or perhaps going out of their way to help a friend in need. And even the most saintly of people might occasionally succumb to urges that they wouldn't wish to have publicized, or otherwise not behave in the manner in which they would prefer. But on average, I'd say that most people fall somewhere in the middle, though with a very wide distribution.

When a particle collides with an antiparticle, they are transformed into energy, Is it true that matter is annihilated and destroyed? Is this literally true? Matter is destroyed? Doesn't this completely contradict the law of conservation of matter? Scientific laws aren't ironclad commandments carved in stone that apply across the totality of existence. Instead, they're useful simplifications, or models, with delimited domains of applicability. Take, for instance, the venerable concept of gravity. Newton's law of universal gravitation is remarkably precise across the scale of everyday interactions, adequately predicting planetary orbits with incredible accuracy. But, as you undoubtedly know, it stumbles somewhat in the vicinity of extreme gravitational fields, like those around a black hole, or even Mercury's orbit, where Einstein's Theory of General Relativity reigns supreme. Yet, despite its imperfections, we routinely use Newton's law, as it is more than sufficient, more often than not. A similar principle holds true for the Law of Conservation of Mass. It serves us well in countless circumstances, from engineering endeavors to balancing chemical equations. However, as Einstein's celebrated equation—E=mc²—elucidates, mass and energy are interchangeable, a concept with profound repercussions. While the energy conversion, with more common elements on Earth, is negligible, a fundamental conversion is happening. The issue arises when we try to apply the Law of Conservation of Mass outside of its valid operational windows. Therefore, it's appropriate to embrace the wider Law of Conservation of Mass-Energy. This, in its most basic form, could be expressed as: E₁ + m₁C² = E₂ + m₂C². If m₂ < m₁, then E₂ will have increased. But the total value of the equation will remain unchanged. Ultimately, nothing is actually destroyed or "annihilated" in the truest sense. Instead, one form of reality is merely being transformed into another.

How can I share the life eternal with those that refuse to view it today? It is like giving someone a check for a billion dollars and they refuse to cash it. What do you do? Do you let them starve and suffer, refusing the gift that would solve all their problems? Or do you just shrug your shoulders and let them walk away? I find myself thinking about this a lot, lately – the people who reject the seemingly obvious benefits, the easy solutions, the clear paths to a better life, whatever that may mean for each individual. It's a frustrating thing, and there is no easy answer. Take, for instance, a friend of mine who adamantly refused to consider any sort of healthcare coverage, even when it was offered to him by a friend for free. He claimed it was because he didn't need it, that he was young and healthy and nothing would ever happen to him. Even when the same friend tried to explain the merits, the protections, and the peace of mind that such coverage provides, he still stubbornly refused, citing a vague distrust based on unfounded rumors. Weeks later, he had the misfortune of an injury, and the costs quickly racked up. Suddenly, health insurance wasn't such a bad idea, and not having it created a much larger problem than he was willing to deal with before. I’ve encountered this phenomenon time and time again, and each situation provides different reasons, excuses, and justifications. People are quick to turn down help, even when the help is truly a gift.

Where does the concept of the Earth being six thousand years old come from? Is it from the Bible? Yes, it's extrapolated from the Bible. The Genesis account in the Bible lists the generations from Adam to Jesus. By adding up the ages of the patriarchs, people have come to the conclusion that the Earth is relatively young, maybe around 6,000 years old. Some specific dates are given by Archbishop James Ussher of Ireland in the mid-17th century, who determined that creation began on October 23, 4004 BC. You'll note that a very specific date is given there – it seems a bit audacious for trying to calculate the age of the Earth, doesn't it? ABOVE: Archbishop James Ussher SOURCE: Wikipedia The scientific community, of course, has largely rejected this, as they have come to a consensus that the Earth is much older, on the order of 4.54 billion years old. This figure is based on all types of evidence - radiometric dating of rocks, the fossil record, and the consistent formation of the solar system, to name a few. Now, it's important to note, that even many religious leaders and thinkers also reject Ussher's timeframe, because the Bible is subject to so many diverse forms of interpretation. For me, at least, it seems that different groups tend to gravitate to whichever interpretation best suits their needs. You also get different interpretations based on how much weight you give to the first couple of chapters of Genesis. Some see it literally, and view it as a straightforward narrative of events, while others see it as a largely allegorical tale. The allegorical interpretation can certainly be quite captivating, but I certainly won't pretend to be an expert in biblical studies – my own familiarity with the subject largely comes from my own church upbringing. But, you can certainly get an appreciation for the diversity of thought by looking up the various schools of theological thought. One particularly fascinating interpretation is known as "the gap theory". Basically, it posits a long gap between the events of Genesis 1:1 and Genesis 1:2. Various scientists and religious thinkers have tried to reconcile the scientific findings with religious beliefs.

Why is the left so adamant in their denial that COVID-19 came from the Wuhan virology lab? It's like a chocolate flood in Hershey, Pennsylvania. Might it be from the candy factory? I haven't delved very deep into the topic, but from what I've seen, the primary cause doesn't seem to be rooted in a single, unifying principle. The left, as a whole, is a large collection of conflicting ideas and opinions. A lot of the fervor seems to be born from simple tribalism, with any ideas from the right being immediately dismissed as false or incorrect, regardless of the evidence. The right has their own share of tribalism as well, of course. Another part, I believe, is distrust of any sources of information. During Trump's presidency, the mainstream media was frequently labeled "fake news," and many of the more sensational claims were found to be false. So it's only natural to distrust anything that comes from the media, and to assume that they're pushing some kind of agenda. Then there's the sheer inconvenience of admitting you were wrong. When the hypothesis gained momentum that it came from the lab, there's no doubt that a number of left wing people were dismissive towards the idea. Not everything always has to be wrong or right in its entirety. Then the information came out that it might be from the lab. Well, now you have to admit, "I was wrong." That's uncomfortable, so some people simply double down in their original belief, rather than admit they were wrong. It's a lot easier. So, I don't think there's any single reason why the left is so hesitant to admit this, but all the factors above probably play a role.

Could you beat up your 20 year old self? It's a fun thought experiment, for sure. I mean, even at my current, older age, I'm not exactly a bastion of physical prowess or anything. I've never even been in a real fight. Aside from a few playground scuffles when I was a kid, my only experience with fisticuffs comes from playing video games or watching movies. And yet, I can't help but think that my hypothetical older self would have a distinct advantage over my younger incarnation. The key here isn't brute strength or youthful agility. It's experience and, dare I say it, wisdom.At 20, I was at the peak of my physical condition, arguably. But I was also a hothead, prone to acting impulsively and making rash decisions. I'd probably get angry and swing blindly, expending all my energy in a chaotic flurry of punches. My older self, on the other hand, would be a lot more calculated and, frankly, boring. I'd know to conserve energy, to observe, to wait for the right moment. I'd target my weak points, utilize my knowledge of human anatomy (thanks, biology class!), and exploit any openings that presented themselves. I'd likely tire my younger self out with a tactical retreat, then patiently pick him off while he was huffing and puffing, trying to catch his breath.So, the short answer is… Yes, I think I *could* beat up my 20-year-old self. It wouldn't be a pretty fight, but it would be a win. I wouldn't necessarily *want* to, though. I'd rather find him, give him a hug, warn of the dangers of youthful indiscretions, and then buy him a beer.

How has technology changed our lives? Technology has fundamentally reshaped our lives, seeping into nearly every facet of existence in ways both subtle and profound. Consider, for instance, the advent of the internet. Not long ago, information access was a laborious process, requiring trips to libraries, encyclopedias, and exhaustive research. Now, with a few keystrokes, we can access an unprecedented wealth of knowledge, spanning the globe and encompassing virtually every topic imaginable. The implications are staggering: educational opportunities have expanded exponentially, communication has become instantaneous, and commerce has been revolutionized. The rise of smartphones and mobile devices further amplified these changes, allowing us to carry this vast repository of information and communication tools in our pockets. We are constantly "connected," tethered to a digital world that offers both incredible convenience and a constant stream of potential distractions. It's hard to remember what life was like before constant connectivity, and yet, here we are - navigating a world where virtual interactions often blur with the physical realm. We navigate a web of apps, social media platforms, and digital services that dictate our schedules, our entertainment, and even our social interactions. The change is not just in *how* we do things, but also in *what* we consider doing in the first place.

Do you eat seafood? What is your favorite fish to eat? I do, indeed. I’m partial to a good, flaky white fish myself. Cod is generally a safe bet – easy enough to cook and nearly universally liked. Had a lovely pan-seared cod fillet just last night, in fact. But, let's be honest, there’s a lot of great fish out there. Salmon is practically a staple, of course; can't really go wrong, especially when done right. I enjoy tuna steaks now and then, though I find they can sometimes be a bit hit or miss, depending on the cut and how it's prepared. Then there’s the more obscure varieties that show up in the fishmonger's case – the ones I might not recognize by name that I'll take a gamble on. I'm always up for trying something new, as long as it looks fresh and the fishmonger seems knowledgeable enough to tell me how to cook it correctly. The only real consideration I have is sustainability. I’ve always tried to be cognizant of where my food comes from, and seafood’s no different. Frankly, all those articles about overfishing in the oceans that I read back in college gave me pause. Still do.
